name: Bekesbourne Aerodrome
text: Your train passes the site of Bekesbourne Aerodrome, on the train's {side}, which had the railway along its northern edge. It began in 1916 as a landing ground for the Royal Flying Corps, and from December 1918 its squadron was commanded by Arthur Harris, later Marshal of the Royal Air Force.

name: St Martin's Church, Canterbury
text: Your train passes near St Martin's Church, on the train's {side}, the oldest church building in England still in use as a church. It was Queen Bertha of Kent's private chapel before Augustine arrived from Rome in 597, and is part of Canterbury's World Heritage Site.

name: Canterbury Castle
text: Your train passes Canterbury Castle, on the train's {side}, one of the three royal castles of Kent built soon after the Battle of Hastings. Its great stone keep went up in the reign of Henry I; by the 19th century a gas company was using it for storage.

name: St Catherine's Church, Preston-next-Faversham
text: Your train passes St Catherine's Church, Preston-next-Faversham, on the train's {side}. It dates from the Norman period, and John Betjeman described it as “high and distinguished among the railways and breweries”.

name: Maison Dieu, Ospringe
text: Your train passes the Maison Dieu at Ospringe, on the train's {side}, beside Watling Street. Henry III commissioned it in 1234 as a hospital and a place for pilgrims and the poor to stay, with a chamber kept for the king to rest in when he passed this way.

name: Church of All Saints, Murston
text: Your train passes near All Saints Church, Murston, on the train's {side}, designed by William Burges and built in 1873 and 1874. Fumes from the brickworks and gasworks round the old church made it hard to breathe during services, so the rector paid £500 of his own money towards a new one away from them.

name: Watling Temple
text: Your train passes near Watling Temple in Newington, on the train's {side}: the remains of a temple in a Roman town found during a dig in 2019, along with pottery kilns and a Roman road. A reconstruction of its foundations, the same size and facing the same way, was unveiled near the spot in 2021.

name: Newington
text: Your train passes Newington, on the train's {side}. Its parish church was built between 1163 and 1177 by Richard de Lucy, and a stone in the church car park, the Devil's Stone, is said to bear the Devil's footprint. The village also holds the national collection of witch hazel.

name: Priestfield Stadium
text: Your train passes near Priestfield Stadium, on the train's {side}, home of Gillingham Football Club since the club began as New Brompton in 1893. Brighton & Hove Albion also played their home games here for two seasons in the 1990s.

name: Chatham Naval Memorial
text: Your train passes near the Chatham Naval Memorial, on the train's {side}, an obelisk on the Great Lines unveiled in 1924. It names sailors and marines of the Royal Navy lost in the First World War who have no known grave, and of the three such memorials (the others are at Portsmouth and Plymouth) it's the only one on a hill.

name: Fort Pitt
text: Your train passes Fort Pitt, on the train's {side}, a fort built between 1805 and 1819 on the high ground between Chatham and Rochester. With the Napoleonic Wars over, it became a military hospital, from 1824 to 1857 the only General Military Hospital in England. Its surviving buildings now house a girls' grammar school.

name: Rochester Castle
text: Your train passes Rochester Castle, on the train's {side}, on the bank of the Medway. Its 12th-century keep, built by William de Corbeil, Archbishop of Canterbury, is one of the best preserved of its time in England or France.

name: St Mildred's Church, Nurstead
text: Your train passes near St Mildred's, the small 14th-century church of Nurstead, on the train's {side}, its walls built of oblong flints. A quarter of a mile north of it is Nurstead Court, called one of the most famous small medieval houses in the country.

name: Longfield
text: Your train passes Longfield, on the train's {side}, recorded as Langanfelda in Saxon charters. In the mid-1940s the planner Patrick Abercrombie proposed building a new town here as part of the Greater London Plan, but other places around London were chosen instead.

name: River Medway (Rochester Bridge)
text: Your train crosses the River Medway on the railway bridge, one of the four bridges that together make up Rochester Bridge. The Romans built the first bridge here to carry Watling Street, and for centuries it was the lowest fixed crossing of the river.

name: Bobbing
text: Your train passes Bobbing, on the train's {side}. In 1673 the local squire made Titus Oates, later the inventor of the Popish Plot, vicar here, but his drunkenness and blasphemy so horrified the parishioners that they put him out before the end of the year.

name: Kemsley
text: Your train passes Kemsley, on the train's {side}, a garden village built in 1924 by Edward Lloyd for the workers at his new Kemsley Paper Mill. The narrow-gauge railway that served the mill survives as the Sittingbourne and Kemsley Light Railway.

name: Ridham Dock
text: Your train passes near Ridham Dock on the Swale, on the train's {side}, planned to give the Sittingbourne paper mills deeper water than the silted Milton Creek. Work began in 1913; during the First World War it was used for loading ammunition, and it was finished in 1919.

name: Kingsferry Bridge
text: Your train crosses the Swale, between the Isle of Sheppey and the mainland, on the Kingsferry Bridge, which carries road and railway together. Its middle span lifts straight up to let ships through; it replaced a bascule bridge of 1860, whose span tipped up instead.

name: Queenborough Castle
text: Your train passes the site of Queenborough Castle, on the train's {side}, built for Edward III from 1361 and named, like the town, after his wife Queen Philippa. It was the first concentric castle built in England; it was pulled down soon after 1650, and only low earthworks remain in what is now a park.

name: St Bartholomew's Church, Goodnestone
text: Your train passes near St Bartholomew's Church, Goodnestone, on the train's {side}, a small Norman church of the 12th century. Its porch had to be rebuilt in 1837 after an earth tremor damaged it; it's now cared for by the Churches Conservation Trust.

name: All Saints Church, Whitstable
text: Your train passes near All Saints Church, Whitstable, on the train's {side}, where there has been a church for at least 800 years. Its oldest brass remembers Thomas Brede, who died in 1444, and a priest's tomb slab still shows the outline of a chalice.

name: Swalecliffe
text: Your train passes Swalecliffe, on the train's {side}, recorded in the Domesday Book. In 1581 a farm here called Bodkin's was given to Gonville and Caius College, Cambridge, and most of its income paid for four scholars.

name: Church of St Mary the Virgin, Reculver
text: Your train passes near the Church of St Mary the Virgin at Hillborough, on the train's {side}, built between 1876 and 1878. It includes materials from the church founded in 669 inside the Roman fort at Reculver, which was mostly pulled down in 1809.

name: Carlton Cinema, Westgate-on-Sea
text: Your train passes near the Carlton Cinema in Westgate-on-Sea, on the train's {side}. It was built in 1910 as the town hall, but within two years it had become a cinema, and it still shows films today.

name: Royal Sea Bathing Hospital
text: Your train passes near the Royal Sea Bathing Hospital in Margate, on the train's {side}, founded in 1791 by the Quaker doctor John Coakley Lettsom to treat poor Londoners with scrofula. Its patients were given fresh air, sunshine and sea bathing, and slept on its verandas whenever the weather allowed.

name: Scenic Railway, Dreamland
text: Your train passes near the Scenic Railway at Dreamland in Margate, on the train's {side}, a wooden roller coaster opened in 1920, with a brakeman riding on each train to control its speed. When it was listed at Grade II* in 2011 it was the oldest working roller coaster in the UK.

name: Dickens House Museum, Broadstairs
text: Your train passes near the Dickens House Museum in Broadstairs, on the train's {side}. The cottage was the home of Mary Pearson Strong, whom Charles Dickens visited on his family holidays here and who inspired Betsey Trotwood in David Copperfield.

name: Montefiore Synagogue
text: Your train passes near the Montefiore Synagogue in Ramsgate, on the train's {side}, the private synagogue Sir Moses Montefiore had built on his estate, finished in 1833. He first came to Ramsgate on his honeymoon in 1812, and his mausoleum stands beside it.

name: St Laurence's Church, Ramsgate
text: Your train passes near St Laurence's Church, on the train's {side}, founded in 1062 and the oldest church in Ramsgate. After lightning struck it in 1439 it was rebuilt, and its tower raised to the height it is today.

name: St Augustine's Cross
text: Your train passes near St Augustine's Cross, on the train's {side}, put up in 1884 to mark Augustine's arrival in England in 597. It's believed to stand where he first met King Ethelbert of Kent.

name: Minster Abbey
text: Your train passes near Minster Abbey, on the train's {side}, founded in about 670 by the Kentish princess Domne Eafe; legend says her land was as much as her pet deer could mark out in a day. Since 1937 Benedictine nuns have lived here, beside the ruins.

name: St Dunstan's Church, Canterbury
text: Your train passes near St Dunstan's Church, on the train's {side}, which dates from the 11th century. In 1174 Henry II changed into sackcloth here before walking to Thomas Becket's tomb in the cathedral, as penance.

name: Church of St Mary, Chartham
text: Your train passes near St Mary's Church, Chartham, on the train's {side}, begun in about 1285, perhaps with the help of Michael of Canterbury, the master mason at Canterbury Cathedral. Its tower was added in the 14th century.

name: Julliberrie's Grave
text: Your train passes near Julliberrie's Grave, on the train's {side}, a long barrow probably built in the fourth millennium BC. No human remains have been found in it, but a broken polished stone axe had been placed at its centre.

name: Godmersham Park
text: Your train passes Godmersham Park, on the train's {side}. Its house, built in 1732, came to Edward Austen Knight, Jane Austen's brother, and she often stayed there.

name: Richborough Roman Fort
text: Your train passes Richborough Roman Fort, on the train's {side}, whose walls still stand several metres high. As Rutupiae it was a main gateway to Roman Britain after the conquest of AD 43 and the start of Watling Street; the coast is now miles away.

name: Deal Castle
text: Your train passes near Deal Castle, on the train's {side}, an artillery fort built by Henry VIII in 1539 and 1540 against invasion from France and the Holy Roman Empire. Its moated stone bastions had 66 firing positions for guns.

name: Old St Mary's Church, Walmer
text: Your train passes near Old St Mary's Church in Upper Walmer, on the train's {side}, built in 1120 as the chapel of Walmer Manor. The Duke of Wellington worshipped here when he stayed at Walmer Castle as Lord Warden of the Cinque Ports, and his hatchment hangs inside.

name: Ripple Mill, Ringwould
text: Your train passes near Ripple Mill, on the train's {side}, a smock mill first built at Drellingore and moved here in the early 19th century, its corner posts cut in half lengthways and bolted back together. Trinity House once helped pay for repairs, as it was a landmark for ships.
